newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Developed states line up to slam trade-labour link.
newsitem.headline: Developed states line up to slam trade-labour link.

text.p: A string of Western nations threw their weight on Monday behind developing countries -- and against the United States -- in their efforts to reject attempts to link trade and labour standards.

Trade ministers from Britain, Australia and Germany all said that the World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting, which began five days of talks on Monday in Singapore, should not discuss issues such as child and slave labour.
British Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang told the WTO's opening session that the International Labour Organisation (ILO) was the right forum for promoting workplace standards.
"While Britain is as strongly opposed to child labour and forced labour as anyone else, we see no case for taking trade measures in support of social standards," Lang said.
He said most of European industry shared this view.
"We know it is also the view of most other countries around the world. Let us not divide the WTO on this issue," he said.
Australian deputy premier and Minister for Trade Tim Fischer later told a news conference that adding labour into the WTO talks could derail its agenda.

"Just because the WTO is one international organisation making real momentum on the planet earth, it doesn't mean everyone else should clip on agendas to hope that the WTO train will carry it forward," he told a news conference.
"If you clip on too many agendas you'll derail the WTO train," he added.
Fischer said Australian experts had recently drawn up a report concluding that sanctions against countries utilising slave labour would be a negative step.

The United States, with the backing of some European countries, wants the contentious issue of labour standards placed on the global trade agenda in a bid to win WTO recognition of basic workers' rights.
But many developing countries fiercely oppose this linkage and fear it could be used as a way of eroding their chief competitive advantage -- cheap labour.
Germany's minister of economics, Guenther Rexrodt, made clear Bonn strongly differed with its EU neighbour France, which supports the United States on the issue.
"We must not bring into the WTO a confrontation about cultural and social values. This would destroy the credibility of the system," he declared in his speech.

"We must ensure that social issues are not used as a pretext for protectionist measures. We, the industrialised countries, have to accept the competitive advantage of less-developed, low wage countries.
"We have to recognise that further liberalisation leads to more prosperity in developing countries, which in turn facilitates the compliance with labour standards," Rexrodt said.
But France's trade minister, Yves Galland, insisted in his opening statement to the WTO that it should begin to study what he called "essential questions", including the labour issue.
"The WTO allows all countries, developed and developing, to express their point of view,' he said.
European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan agreed. He told the meeting trade was now a domestic political issue in all countries.
"For me this means that concerns about environment, about labour standards and other apparently domestic political issues are now the legitimate concern of the WTO," he said.
